Supervised adaptation and LoRA

How do supervised examples change a pretrained language model? Follow the response-token loss from the prompt boundary to a parameter update, then use low-rank adaptation to train a small update while preserving the base weights.

Worked examples use small constructed numbers to show the mechanics.

Microlecture 1

From prompting to supervised adaptation

Instructor: Video · Slides (PDF)

AI-generated version: Video · Slides (PDF)

The closing question in the ML01 video previews a topic that this page no longer covers. Continue with Microlecture 2: Instruction data and evaluation.

Instruction fine-tuning

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) continues training a pretrained model on labelled input–target pairs. It includes supervised adaptation for tasks such as classification and translation.

Instruction fine-tuning is a form of SFT that uses instructions and target responses to train instruction following across tasks and languages. J&M use “SFT” for this instruction–response training in §8.1.

The running translation example

Request: Translate “No tenía lavandería” into English. Return only the translation.

Base response: Output: It didn’t have a laundry facility.
Response after instruction SFT: It didn’t have a laundry facility.

Both responses preserve the translation. The response after instruction SFT follows the requested output format. In Block 1, Microlecture 6, we revised the prompt to improve format compliance. Instruction SFT trains on target responses.

Recall from Block 1: ordinary prompting changes the context while model weights stay fixed. Supervised fine-tuning uses examples to update selected parameters; those updates remain available on later requests.

Pretraining, in-context learning and instruction SFT

Pretraining (Block 1, ML5)ICL (Block 1, ML3–4)Instruction SFT
DataBroad text sequences, such as documents.Instruction, demonstrations and current input in the prompt.Curated prompt–response pairs.
Tokens with training lossEligible next-token targets across the text; padding is excluded.None during ordinary inference.Response targets only; prompt and padding targets are excluded.
How the example actsActivations and loss gradients.Activations; no parameter update.Activations and loss gradients.
What persists as learned parameters?Updated model weights.No newly learned parameters.Updated weights or adapter factors.

SFT uses the same next-token cross-entropy objective introduced in Block 1, Microlecture 5, with supervised response targets. Here, “SFT” in the table means instruction SFT; other supervised adaptation setups may use different targets or masks. In ICL, text and cached context can remain available while retained, but demonstrations do not create a learned parameter update.

A demonstration in a prompt helps condition a later answer through the forward computation. A target response in a training pair supplies prediction errors that produce parameter gradients. Use the example as prompt context during ICL or as supervised targets during SFT.

Hindi–English example

Hindi: यहाँ एक पुस्तकालय है।
English: There is a library here.

For ICL, put this completed pair in the prompt before a new input, such as यहाँ एक अस्पताल है। For SFT, use the library sentence as input and its English translation as the target response. ICL uses the completed pair as context. SFT computes loss on the English target response.

Sources: J&M §8.1, pp. 210–211, Figs. 8.1–8.2; §8.2, pp. 213–215.

Microlecture 2

Instruction data and evaluation

Instructor: Video · Slides (PDF)

AI-generated version: Video · Slides (PDF)

Instruction tuning needs many instruction–response pairs. Figure 8.2 showed four of them. A useful dataset covers thousands of tasks and many languages. The first problem is supply: where do millions of good pairs come from? The second problem is measurement. Instruction tuning aims at instruction following in general, so we must test the model on tasks it did not train on.

How large are instruction datasets?

DatasetExamplesCoverage
Aya513 million instructions12 tasks; 114 languages
Super-NaturalInstructions5 million examples1,600 tasks
Flan 202215 million examples1,836 tasks
OPT-IML18 million examples2,000 tasks

These collections span thousands of tasks. Writing every pair by hand would be slow and costly.

Pairs written by people

Aya’s human-written subset contains 204,000 instruction–response instances, written by 3,000 fluent speakers of 65 languages. J&M note that producing high-quality data this way is time-consuming and costly.

Pairs converted from NLP datasets

A cheaper source is the large body of existing supervised datasets, such as SQuAD for question answering. Each record already holds task fields and a ground-truth label (Figure 8.3). The fields are extracted as key/value pairs and inserted into instruction templates (Figure 8.4). Language models then paraphrase the templates, so the instructions vary in wording.

Pairs generated by language models

J&M describe this as the most common route. Bianchi et al. began with datasets of harmful questions. A language model paraphrased the questions and wrote safe responses. People reviewed the generated responses before adding them to the dataset.

The review matters because SFT trains the model to imitate each target, including its errors. Bianchi et al. found that 500 such safety instructions, mixed into a large instruction dataset, substantially reduced harmful responses.

Annotation guidelines can also serve as prompts. Figure 8.5 shows a crowdworker guideline from NaturalInstructions used to generate examples.

Why generate data with a trained model?

The model that generates the data is usually different from the model being trained. Three reasons make generated data useful.

  • Distillation. A large, aligned model writes the responses. A smaller or base model trains on them. The capability already exists in the generator’s weights, and SFT copies it into the student’s weights. Figure 8.2 draws on Alpaca: its 52,000 instruction–response pairs were generated with OpenAI’s text-davinci-003 and used to fine-tune LLaMA 7B.
  • From the prompt into the weights. A generator can write a good response when its prompt contains a long guideline, such as Figure 8.5, or an explicit request to answer safely. The student trains on the short instruction and that response, with the guideline left out. This is called context distillation (Askell et al., 2021). In Microlecture 1, a demonstration helped only while it stayed in the prompt. Here the behaviour persists in the parameters.
  • Review is cheaper than writing. People check the generated responses. Checking costs much less than writing every response by hand. Bianchi et al. reviewed their generated responses manually.

The chain begins with human data. Early instruction-tuned models were trained on converted datasets and human-written demonstrations. Later models use these models to generate data.

Limits of generated data

  • The student inherits the teacher’s limits. SFT imitates each target, including its errors. Gudibande et al. trained open models to imitate ChatGPT. The imitation models copied its style closely. They closed little of the gap in factual accuracy, and human raters were partly misled by the style.
  • Closed loops degrade models. Suppose each generation of a model trains only on outputs from the previous generation. Shumailov et al. showed that the rare cases in the data then disappear first, and quality declines. They called this model collapse. Keeping real data in the mix and filtering generated data guard against it.
  • Quality matters more than quantity. LIMA fine-tuned a 65-billion-parameter model on 1,000 carefully curated examples and obtained strong instruction following. Bianchi et al.’s 500 reviewed safety examples point the same way.

Generated data works well for transferring behaviour from a stronger model. It also works well for moving prompted behaviour into the weights. It cannot supply knowledge that the generator lacks. Used in a closed loop without real data or review, it degrades the model.

Evaluating instruction following

This completes the supply problem. The second problem is measurement. A fair test uses tasks the model never saw during instruction tuning. The standard method is leave-one-out: tune on a large set of tasks, then test on a withheld task.

Similar tasks complicate this. Super-NaturalInstructions contains 25 separate textual-entailment datasets. Withholding one of them would leave 24 related datasets in training. J&M therefore group datasets into clusters by task similarity. Textual entailment (NLI) forms one cluster. They then withhold a whole cluster. The same rule applies to any cluster.

Sentiment as the withheld cluster

Remove every sentiment dataset from the instruction-tuning data. Tune on the remaining clusters. Test on the withheld sentiment datasets. Records like the sentiment example in Figure 8.3 then appear only at test time.

Sources: J&M §8.1.1–8.1.2, pp. 211–213, Figs. 8.2–8.5. Taori et al. (2023); Gudibande et al. (2024); Shumailov et al. (2024); Zhou et al. (2023).

Microlecture 3

The cost of full fine-tuning

Instructor: Video · Slides (PDF)

AI-generated version: Video · Slides (PDF)

Instruction tuning is a special case of a general need. We often want to adapt a pretrained model to a new task, a new domain or a new language. The pretraining data covers many domains, but some data, such as instructions, may not appear often enough. We may also want a model specialised to legal or medical text, or one that is better at a particular language.

Fine-tuning in general

Fine-tuning continues training a pretrained model on new data. The loss is the same cross-entropy used in pretraining. Instruction tuning treats the instruction as context and trains on the response tokens only. Other fine-tuning may train on every token of the new data. Fine-tuning can update all the parameters, some of them, or only added parameters.

Why full fine-tuning is expensive

Full fine-tuning updates every parameter. Each training step runs a forward pass through every layer, backpropagates the loss through every layer, computes a gradient for every parameter and then updates every parameter. A large language model has billions of parameters and many large layers.

The cost appears in processing power, in memory and in time. Fine-tuning data is far smaller than pretraining data, but the model is the same size. Many labs cannot fine-tune all the parameters of the largest models.

Block 1, Microlectures 7–8, used C ≈ 6ND to estimate training compute in FLOPs. The estimate below counts stored training state in bytes. Memory and compute are different quantities.

A memory estimate

Use the Adam optimizer with 32-bit floating point numbers. Each trainable parameter then needs four stored values of 4 bytes each.

Stored for each parameterBytes
Weight4
Gradient4
Adam first moment4
Adam second moment4
Total16

A 7-billion-parameter model

7 × 10⁹ parameters × 16 bytes ≈ 112 GB. The weights alone take 7 × 10⁹ × 4 bytes = 28 GB.

One 80 GB GPU cannot hold this training state. Activations for backpropagation add more memory on top.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) freezes most of the parameters and updates a small selected subset. Frozen parameters keep their pretrained values. Gradients and optimizer state are needed only for the selected subset. The frozen parameters still take part in every forward pass.

LoRA is the most common PEFT method. A transformer has many dense layers that multiply by a weight matrix, such as WQ, WK, WV and WO in attention. LoRA freezes these matrices and trains a small low-rank update for each one.

Sources: J&M §8.2, pp. 213–215, Fig. 8.6; Kingma and Ba (2015).

Microlecture 4

Low-rank adaptation

Instructor: Video · Slides (PDF)

AI-generated version: Video · Slides (PDF)

Microlecture 3 ended with a question: how can a small update change a large matrix? Consider one weight matrix W of shape k × d, such as an attention projection. Full fine-tuning gives W an update ΔW of the same shape, so the update has k × d entries. Every entry needs a gradient and two Adam moments.

From ΔW to two thin matrices

LoRA, for low-rank adaptation, freezes W. It trains two matrices instead: A, of shape k × r, and B, of shape r × d. The rank r is much smaller than k and d. LoRA replaces W + ΔW with W + AB. The product AB has shape k × d, the same as W, so the two can be added.

Rank of an update

The rank of a matrix is the number of linearly independent rows, which equals the number of linearly independent columns. It counts the independent directions in the matrix. Take a LoRA update with k = 4, d = 3 and r = 1:

A =
1
2
0
−1
B =
2−13
AB =
2−13
4−26
000
−21−3

Every row of AB is a multiple of B. Every column of AB is a multiple of A. So AB has rank 1. It has 4 × 3 = 12 entries, built from 4 + 3 = 7 values. Microlecture 5 uses these A and B in a forward pass.

In general, every row of AB is a combination of the r rows of B. So rank(AB) ≤ r. A small r keeps the update in a small number of directions.

The LoRA forward pass

A dense layer computes h = xW for an input row vector x. With LoRA, the forward pass becomes

h = xW + xAB (J&M Eq. 8.1)
QuantityShape
x1 × k
xA1 × r
xAB = (xA)B1 × d
xW1 × d
h = xW + xAB1 × d

W stays frozen. A and B are trained directly from the task loss. For instruction tuning, that is the response-token cross-entropy from Microlecture 1. Only the update has rank at most r. The sum W + AB can be full rank, and Microlecture 5 shows an example.

How many parameters are trained?

ΔW: kd entries
A and B: kr + rd = r(k + d) entries

One 4096 × 4096 matrix, r = 8

Full update: 4096 × 4096 = 16,777,216 entries.
LoRA: 8 × (4096 + 4096) = 65,536 entries.
Ratio: 65,536 / 16,777,216 = 1/256.

W still stores its 16,777,216 frozen entries. Gradients and Adam moments are needed only for the 65,536 trained entries.

The original LoRA was applied to the attention matrices WQ, WK, WV and WO. Many variants of LoRA exist. The trainable count for a model is the sum over the adapted matrices.

From here on we write W₀ for the frozen pretrained matrix.

Sources: J&M §8.2, pp. 214–215, Eq. 8.1, Figs. 8.7–8.8; Hu et al., §4.

Microlecture 5

A worked LoRA example

Instructor: Video · Slides (PDF)

AI-generated version: Video · Slides (PDF)

Take one layer with k = 4 inputs, d = 3 outputs and rank r = 1. W₀ is the frozen pretrained matrix. A and B are the factors from Microlecture 4, after some training. We compute h with Eq. 8.1, h = xW₀ + xAB. We then compute the gradients that training needs for A and B, and take one gradient step.

x =
10−12
W₀ =
100
010
001
111
A =
1
2
0
−1
B =
2−13

Forward computation

  1. Base branch: xW₀ = row 1 − row 3 + 2 × row 4 = [1+2, 0+2, −1+2] = [3, 2, 1].
  2. First factor: u = xA = 1×1 + 0×2 + (−1)×0 + 2×(−1) = −1.
  3. Second factor: uB = (−1)[2, −1, 3] = [−2, 1, −3].
  4. Sum: h = [3, 2, 1] + [−2, 1, −3] = [1, 3, −2].

The adapter branch passes through a single number, u, because r = 1. LoRA trains 4 + 3 = 7 entries in this layer. A dense update of W₀ has 12.

Gradients through the adapter

Backpropagation delivers g = ∂L/∂h, a 1 × d row, to the output of this layer. Three rules of backpropagation give every gradient we need.

  • Product. For y = zM: ∇ML = zᵀ(∂L/∂y) and ∂L/∂z = (∂L/∂y)Mᵀ.
  • Sum. For y = a + b: ∂L/∂a = ∂L/∂b = ∂L/∂y.
  • Shared input. If z enters two products, ∂L/∂z is the sum of the two contributions.

Write the layer as h = xW₀ + uB, with u = xA. It contains three products: uB, xA and xW₀. The sum sends g to both branches. The input x enters two products, xA and xW₀.

Applying the rules product by product

Work backwards from the output. Each row uses the product rule once.

ProductzM∂L/∂y∇ML = zᵀ(∂L/∂y)∂L/∂z = (∂L/∂y)Mᵀ
uBuBg∇BL = uᵀg (r × d)∂L/∂u = gBᵀ (1 × r)
xAxAgBᵀ∇AL = xᵀ(gBᵀ) (k × r)gBᵀAᵀ
xW₀xW₀gxᵀg: not computed, W₀ is frozengW₀ᵀ

The gradient at u from the first row becomes ∂L/∂y in the second row. That is how the gradient reaches A through B. The shared-input rule then adds the two contributions at x:

∂L/∂x = gW₀ᵀ + gBᵀAᵀ (1 × k)

The frozen W₀ still passes the gradient back to earlier layers. Its own gradient xᵀg is not needed, because W₀ is not updated.

Gradient calculation and parameter update

The example with g = [1, 0, −1]

u = xA = −1, so ∇BL = (−1)[1, 0, −1] = [−1, 0, 1].
gBᵀ = 1×2 + 0×(−1) + (−1)×3 = −1, so ∇AL = (−1)xᵀ = [−1, 0, 1, −2]ᵀ.
∂L/∂x = [1, 0, −1, 0] + [−1, −2, 0, 1] = [0, −2, −1, 1].

Full fine-tuning would need ∇W₀L = xᵀg, a 4 × 3 matrix with 12 entries. LoRA stores 4 + 3 = 7.

One gradient step with learning rate η = 0.1

A ← A − η∇AL = [1.1, 2, −0.1, −0.8]ᵀ.
B ← B − η∇BL = [2.1, −1, 2.9].

The new xA is −0.4, so h becomes [3, 2, 1] − 0.4[2.1, −1, 2.9] = [2.16, 2.4, −0.16]. The change is Δh = [1.16, −0.6, 1.84], and g · Δh = −0.68. The first-order change in loss is negative.

Merging the LoRA update

AB has the same size as W₀, so it can be added to the pretrained weights:

W₀ + AB =
3−13
4−16
001
−12−2

Then x(W₀ + AB) = [3, −1, 3] − [0, 0, 1] + [−2, 4, −4] = [1, 3, −2], the same h as the two-branch computation. Inference with the merged matrix takes no extra time. LoRA modules for different domains can be swapped in and out by adding or subtracting their AB. Each adapter works only with the base model it was trained on.

Here rank(AB) = 1 and rank(W₀ + AB) = 3. Adding the rank-1 update leaves the effective matrix full rank.

Sources: J&M §8.2, pp. 214–215, Eq. 8.1; Hu et al.

Block 2 recap

We began with a fixed-weight model responding to a prompt. Supervised adaptation uses target responses to change selected parameters. LoRA retains the base model and learns a small factorized update.

IdeaWhat to retain
Training signalInstruction SFT uses conditional response-token cross-entropy. Prompt tokens remain context.
Data and evaluationConstruct instruction pairs from datasets, human contributions and model generation. Evaluate on withheld task clusters.
Training costFull fine-tuning stores a weight, a gradient and two Adam moments for every parameter: 16 bytes each at 32-bit precision. PEFT freezes most parameters and trains a subset.
LoRA updateΔW = AB with A: k × r and B: r × d, so rank(AB) ≤ r and r(k + d) entries are trained. W₀ stays frozen.
Worked computationxW₀ = [3, 2, 1]; xAB = [−2, 1, −3]; h = [1, 3, −2]. The gradients ∇BL = uᵀg and ∇AL = xᵀ(gBᵀ) follow from the product rule.
MergingW₀ + AB gives the same h with no extra inference time. An adapter needs the base model it was trained on.

How can we update a language model when the training signal is a reward for a generated response, rather than a target response to imitate?

These are printed page numbers; PDF pages are 218–223. Textbook website (the online draft can change).
  • Hu et al., LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. 2021 preprint; ICLR 2022. §§4.1–4.2 support the update formulation, initialization, scale, choice of target matrices and merge discussion. Paper · Version 2, Section 4. The paper’s column-vector BA convention is translated to J&M’s row-vector AB convention here.
  • Taori et al., Alpaca: A Strong, Replicable Instruction-Following Model. Stanford CRFM, 2023. 52,000 instruction–response pairs generated with text-davinci-003; LLaMA 7B fine-tuned on them. Project page · Repository.
  • Askell et al., A General Language Assistant as a Laboratory for Alignment. 2021. Introduces context distillation. Paper.
  • Gudibande et al., The False Promise of Imitating Proprietary LLMs. ICLR 2024. Imitation models copy style more than factual accuracy. Paper.
  • Shumailov et al., AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data. Nature 631 (2024). Model collapse under recursive training on generated data. Paper.
  • Kingma and Ba, Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization. ICLR 2015. The optimizer whose two moment estimates enter the memory estimate in Microlecture 3. Paper.
  • Rajbhandari et al., ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models. SC 2020. Counts 16 bytes per parameter for mixed-precision Adam training. Paper.
  • Zhou et al., LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment. NeurIPS 2023. Instruction following from 1,000 curated examples. Paper.
